title: Clinical significance and pathogenesis of portal HTN
guide: Portal HTN can manifest with or without cirrhosis and leads to hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites (1st sign of decompensation) → hepatorenal syndrome; jaundice + liver failure = decompensation with average survival without transplant printed as ‘a years’ (≈1 year) versus mean survival of 12 years without decompensation/transplant. Pathogenesis: portal venous pressure ≥ 12 mm Hg, sinusoidal pressure ≥ 6 mm Hg (clinically significant ≥ 10 mm Hg); cirrhosis (loss of fenestration, compression by nodules, ↑ septae) raises splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). The cirrhotic sinusoid diagram: collagen deposition in space of Disse, activation of hepatic stellate cells, constriction and defenestration of sinusoids; nodules and fibrous septae compress sinusoids → ↑ portal → ↑ splenic vein pressure (caput medusae = back flow of blood from portal veins).

title: Hepatic vasculature: the portal vein
guide: Portal vein: development — inferior segment of left and right vitelline veins joins to form it; formation — splenic vein + superior mesenteric vein join behind the neck of pancreas, 7.5 cm long, hilum posterior to hepatic (artery) and bile duct. High compliance, low resistance. Branching diagram: umbilical vein drains into left portal vein, cystic vein into right portal vein, 1st order = main trunk, 3rd order (Bifurcation), ‘…rd order (Entry)’ label garbled in print. Hepatic buffer response: hepatic ischaemia is rare d/t dual blood supply (portal vein, hepatic artery).

title: Sinusoidal vasoconstriction and the HVPG ladder
guide: Resistance due to (P = F × R; R↑ = P↑): mechanical — nodule compressing sinusoid; functional — ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration. HVPG table: 1–5 mm Hg normal; ≥ 10 mm Hg clinically significant portal hypertension; ≥ 12 mm Hg threshold for variceal rupture; ≥ 20 mm Hg ↑ risk of death.

title: Causes of portal HTN: pre-hepatic, post-hepatic, intrahepatic
guide: Pre-hepatic: 1st order portal vein occlusion AKA EHPVO — seen in 3–8 yr olds; severe upper GI bleed, massive splenomegaly, no cirrhosis (good prognosis); causes umbilical sepsis, splenic vein thrombosis (rare). Post-hepatic: (a) hepatic vein obstruction AKA Budd–Chiari (classical: ascites + hepatomegaly); (b) right heart failure — tricuspid regurgitation, restrictive cardiomyopathy, constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP). Intrahepatic (3rd order portal vein): pre-sinusoidal — NCPF/idiopathic portal hypertension (young adult, upper GI bleed, splenomegaly, cirrhosis rare), schistosomiasis, sarcoidosis; post-sinusoidal — sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/veno-occlusive disease a/w post-hematopoietic stem cell transplant following myeloablative alkylating therapy, symptoms 10–30 days after; sinusoidal — cirrhosis.

title: Work-up of portal HTN and the WHVP/FHVP/HVPG table
guide: Flow: patient with risk factors for chronic hepatitis → deranged LFT + USG (fatty liver + negative serology, AST/ALT < 150) → confirms chronic hepatitis (NASH) → Fibroscan 13.5 kPa → cirrhosis → splenomegaly (+), ↓ platelet → portal HTN (+) → quantity with HVPG / endoscopy. HVPG = WHVP − FHVP (expansion line prints ‘FWVP: free hepatic venous pressure’). Table: prehepatic & presinusoidal — all normal; sinusoidal & postsinusoidal — WHVP ↑, FHVP normal, HVPG ↑; unlabeled row — WHVP ↑, FHVP ↑ (hepatic vein cannot be cannulated), HVPG normal. HVPG > 10 mm Hg → Rx non-selective β-blocker carvedilol (best).

title: Endoscopy, EVL indications and modified Child–Pugh
guide: Endoscopy: large varices → non-selective β-blocker carvedilol (best); mild/moderate varices → conservative management. Indications for endoscopic variceal ligation: intolerant to β-blocker therapy (asthma, COPD); β-blockers contraindicated (severe bradycardia); target HVPG not achieved with β-blocker. Modified Child–Pugh: parameters — ascites, encephalopathy, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time (seconds increased); classes A, B, C with B + C bracketed as ‘requires transplant’.

title: Variceal bleeds: determinants and natural history
guide: Main factor: variceal wall tension, determined by vessel diameter + pressure, directly related to HVPG. Causes/epidemiology: gastric esophageal varices 50% cause cirrhosis (as printed); without-varices development rate 8%/year; variceal hemorrhage occurrence 5–15%/year; risk of bleeding — small varices (≤ 5 mm) < 10%/year, large varices 30%/year; mortality from variceal bleeding 15–30%.

title: Acute variceal bleeding: the step-ladder
guide: Bleeding → a large bore IV cannulas; terlipressin (1st) stat dose → 2 mg Q6h × 48 hours (print shows ‘a mg’); alternative (>) IV octreotide 50 µg stat → 50 µg/hour; box — start antibiotics, replace blood volume, intubation to be considered; upon failure → endoscopy: variceal ligation or sclerotherapy; upon failure → TIPSS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt).
